01

The challenge

Why the visual language needed to evolve

As Digit's digital ecosystem expanded, the visual language needed to evolve with it. The brand moved from flat 2D illustrations and line icons to a more expressive, dimensional and cohesive 3D system.

Digit already had a recognisable style, but as products and touchpoints grew, the ecosystem held multiple styles at once — line icons, filled illustrations and independently created assets — making consistency hard to maintain at scale.

Before — line icons and independently created 2D assets

Visual consistency

One recognisable language across insurance categories and digital journeys.

Scalability

Support a fast-growing feature library without redesigning the language each time.

Product relevance

Visuals suited to modern app and website interfaces.

Brand recognition

A distinctive use of yellow, charcoal and dimensional form.

Emotional connection

Insurance communication that feels warmer and less transactional.

02

The evolution

Evolving the system — not just the style

The transition happened progressively: line icons, then 2D illustrations, then 3D exploration with depth, material and lighting — and finally a systemised language with rules that could be replicated across categories.

2D line
→
Systemised 3D
2D line
→
Systemised 3D
Flat→Dimensional
Functional→Expressive
Individual assets→Visual system
Decorative graphics→Product storytelling

The 3D treatment had to stay simple enough for insurance communication while adding warmth, recognition and personality.

03

Building the system

A system before a library

Rather than designing each icon independently, I established repeatable principles so new assets would feel like part of the same family — simple, optimistic, helpful, human and trustworthy.

Simple

One clear idea per icon with minimal supporting elements.

Optimistic

Warm forms, soft geometry and Digit's signature yellow.

Helpful

The feature or insurance concept reads immediately.

Human

Friendly proportions rather than highly technical forms.

Trustworthy

Controlled compositions that hold the credibility insurance requires.

The result stays recognisable even when the subject changes from health and travel to motor, payments, claims or support.

04

The visual rules

Creating consistency at scale

To make the system repeatable, I defined guidelines around colour, form, material, perspective, lighting and composition.

#FFBB00

Amber · 80%

Primary brand colour and visual hero

#444444

Charcoal · 15%

Structure, depth and contrast

#FFFFFF

White · 5%

Clarity and breathing room

The palette was intentionally restricted so every asset reads as Digit at a glance.

Form language

  • Rounded geometry, soft edges
  • Slightly inflated, friendly proportions
  • No sharp corners or heavy detail

Perspective

  • Consistent 3/4 view
  • Slight top angle, 20°–30°
  • No dramatic camera angles

Material & lighting

  • Soft matte polymer, satin finish
  • Soft studio light, warm neutral
  • No chrome, glass, metallic or neon

Composition & shadow

  • 3–5 components, one clear hero
  • Soft contact shadows, grounded
  • No floating icons or long shadows

Clarity always comes before decoration.

06

From icons to illustrations

Extending the system into storytelling

The same principles expanded beyond compact icons into larger illustrations for key product moments — balancing human characters, functional objects and insurance cues while keeping the composition visually light.

A recognisable visual grammar

Recurring cues connect different stories: the umbrella for protection, shield and checkmark for trust and completion, the policy folder for documents, yellow coins for value, sparks for optimism and charcoal devices for digital functionality. These recombine by message instead of being reinvented per feature.

07

In the product

Live in the Digit App

The illustrations were introduced within onboarding and login moments, communicating key app benefits before users entered the product — the illustration carrying the story while the interface stays clean.

Instant policy renewals

Challan & PUC expiry

Wellness benefits

10+ exclusive features

Policy documents 24×7

08

Designed for product, not decoration

The visuals had to work inside UI

Every asset had to hold up at real product sizes, alongside typography, navigation and interaction.

Hierarchy

The main concept stays identifiable instantly.

Responsive composition

Illustrations survive cropping and different device dimensions.

Visual weight

Enough depth to feel dimensional without overpowering the UI.

Whitespace

Supporting elements preserve space for copy and actions.

Small-screen legibility

Fine detail reduced so icons read on mobile.

Carousel consistency

Shared frames, proportions and colour create continuity across onboarding.

09

System thinking

Designing for the next 100 icons

The value was not a fixed number of assets. It was rules that made the next icon easier to design than the last — and a language that could move between app interfaces, website experiences, product communication and marketing.

A new visual could now be evaluated against a shared framework:

  • Does it use the correct perspective?
  • Does it follow the approved palette?
  • Is there one clear visual hero?
  • Can the concept be understood at a small size?
  • Does it use the same material and lighting language?
  • Does it feel unmistakably Digit?

This turned the work from individual illustration production into visual system design.

10

Contribution & impact

What changed, and my part in it

A more unified experience

Varied illustration styles moved towards one recognisable language.

Stronger recognition

Digit Yellow became more intentional and distinctive in product visuals.

Greater scalability

New feature icons follow established rules instead of starting from scratch.

My contribution

  • Exploring the shift from existing 2D assets into a 3D visual direction.
  • Creating and refining 3D insurance icons across multiple categories.
  • Establishing consistency in colour, perspective, lighting and material.
  • Creating human-centred 3D illustrations for larger product moments.
  • Applying the system to real Digit App experiences and website requirements.
  • Defining visual guidelines to make the style easier to scale.

The project let me work beyond individual asset creation and contribute to how Digit's digital brand could look, feel and scale as a system.

The most meaningful part was not one successful icon — it was a system capable of producing hundreds of them.
